newsitem.title: USA: Character issue keeps bubbling up in Dole campaign.
newsitem.headline: Character issue keeps bubbling up in Dole campaign.

text.p: Bob Dole likened himself to "plain-spoken" and honest Presidents Harry Truman and Dwight Eisenhower on Friday as the struggles within his campaign over how aggressively to attack President Clinton's ethics and character spilled into the open.

Campaigning for the second day by bus in Ohio, Dole pressed the theme of his own trustworthiness versus President Clinton's penchant for breaking promises without wading into the problematic "character issue".
Each time the Republican Dole ignores an invitation to attack Clinton, the character issue gets rehashed in the media without Dole risking being portrayed as a villain.

Underscoring the ambivalence within the campaign over whether the underdog Dole should go on the offensive, campaign vice chairman Bill Bennett announced a game plan to ratchet up the attack next week on the Clinton administration's ethical record.
"I think we are going too easy on them, given what they deserve," Bennett, a former Secretary of Education, told reporters aboard the campaign bus caravan through Ohio.

"I'm not talking about the trailer park stuff, I'm not talking about philandering," Bennett said, ticking off a list of allegations, investigations and scandals including Whitewater, the "Travelgate" probe, White House staff access to confidential FBI files and some of Hillary Rodham Clinton's past legal work.
"These are not pecadillos, these are not small things," said Bennett, adding that even if some personal character issues should be off limits, these are in the realm of public morality.

But another senior campaign aide, who asked not to be named, denied that any such strategic shift had been agreed upon. "Bill Bennett was charting one path the campaign may take but the ultimate decisions has not been made yet by Bob Dole," the aide said.

Dole himself stuck to his message of trust and honesty as he wooed Ohio's 21 electoral votes, attracting warm crowds and appearing to be enjoying himself in the scenic small towns, farms and campuses.

"I'm a plain-spoken man. I'm sort of like Harry Truman and Ike Eisenhower and others that you're aware of," the former Kansas senator told one rally on Friday. "We're not as articulate or whatever, but we like to tell the truth, and we feel bad if we don't tell the truth."

"We feel bad if we look you in the eye and say we're going to cut your taxes and then we raise your taxes," Dole said at the University of Findlay, one of several appearances where he reminded people of Clinton's 1992 unfulfilled pledge to cut middle-class taxes.
Truman was a Democrat and Eisenhower a Republican, but they both represent the nostalgic images that Dole, 73, often evokes of a happier and safer mid-century America.

At another rally in Lima, he predicted that on Nov. 5 people would enter voting booths and ask themselves, "Which one of these men ... can I trust? And they're going to say Bob Dole, Bob Dole, Bob Dole."

Dole's campaign was buoyed by a few opinion polls that showed the race is narrowing. The Field poll in California showed the two candidates 10 points apart, a big difference from the 22 percent in late summer. And the Reuters tracking poll on Friday put the difference between Clinton and Dole at 9.7 percentage points.
But other polls show a larger gap, and Dole clearly has an uphill struggle.
Asked whether an aggressive offence would be seen as a desparate ploy by a candidate still lagging in the polls, Bennett replied, "I don't think it's negative, I don't think it's desperate."
"I don't feel either negative or desparate, I feel frustrated," he added. "I believe this administration is one of the most corrupt in recent American history."
